utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, October 1st, 2008, and I welcome our witness as well as the accused, counsels for Defence and Mr. Kruger and Mr. Scott and all his team from the OTP as well -- and I also welcome all the other people helping us in this courtroom. I will soon give -- I will now give the floor to the registrar he has an IC number to communicate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 1D has submitted its objections to documents tendered by the Prosecution through Witness Kozulj, Ilija. This list shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00859. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, I believe that the witness has a problem with his mike. Witness, can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now for the cross-examination. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, sir. Good morning to the Judges, everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Palameta. My name is Pieter Kruger --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- and I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor, as you've no doubt gathered. Sir, if we can start just with a few general matters. The first thing I'd like to hear from you is it wasn't very clear on Monday about where you were living during various periods that we were talking about. Now, is it correct, first of all, that before April 1992 you were actually working in Mostar -- sorry, in --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In Mostar, and did you go home weekends to your home in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to correct you. Before April 1992, I was working both in Mostar and in Sarajevo. I worked in Sarajevo for almost a year before April 1992. Would you repeat the rest of your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly. During the -- that period we're talking about now, did you only live in Stolac at your home during the weekends --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The rest of the time were you living in Sarajevo or in Mostar? This is prior to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before April 1992 I was in Sarajevo for little less than a year, and during that time I was not in Mostar. I was in Sarajevo and I would come to Stolac to my home for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your home in Stolac, was that in the town of Stolac itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From April 1992 to the end of 1992, did you then live constantly in your home in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April 1992 I didn't live in my home at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court how that came about. That was when you left Stolac during the Serb occupation, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. After the 13th - I'm not sure of the exact date - we left Stolac. My family had left a day or two previously and we lived at different addresses. My parents and my wife and children were in Grac -- in Gradac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small town on the Croatian coast where most of the refugees from Stolac were concentrated at that time. Sometimes I stayed with them and sometimes I stayed at other addresses mostly in the Primorje region or in Herzegovina on the unoccupied territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You returned to Stolac in June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats returned to Stolac in 1992, but I did not return in full. I only visited Stolac for a -- well, for a few days about five times, on about five occasions that summer. I was not in Stolac often. I was in the Stolac municipality and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The elsewhere, could you perhaps just give the Court an idea what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed with my parents when they returned. I was with my wife and children in Gradac, I was in Neum, I was in Zagreb, in various places where I was able to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during 1993 could you give the Court an idea of where you were living at that stage -- rather, I'll simplify it. Did you live or from time to time at least go to Stolac during 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1993 I can remember being in Stolac only once, sometime in January or February, and after that in the late summer perhaps when I passed through Stolac. At that time I was mostly with my students in Neum, especially during the second semester; before that, I was in Mostar, where I worked in the subdepartment for education. I was in Visici, for example. Sometimes I would spend the night with my aunt in Visici. That's what I can remember right now, but in that period I didn't have much reason to go to Stolac. I was oriented towards other business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. You went to Stolac in the late summer of 1993. When was that? Would that have been in August? September?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, Mr. Jadranko Prlic, you knew him personally during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And later, when you were appointed as ambassador to Rome, that was in 1997, was Mr. Prlic at that stage the minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did he appoint you as ambassador then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think he could not do that at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps just returning very briefly to the issue of where you were living during 1993. As -- working in the subdepartment for education, did you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- did you have to regularly attend meetings in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Mostar where my office was as often as possible. It may not have been every day, but I went there very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you also have an apartment or a home in Mostar at that -- during that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you stay anywhere in Mostar for any periods of time during 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with some relatives of mine. I had relatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was that in the city of Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can just move to a few things to clear up from your evidence the other day. Do you recall that on Monday you were shown two documents which were decrees, the first one on secondary education in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the document I'm referring to is 1D 0019. That's the decree on secondary and primary education in Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna -- sorry, on secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the decree on secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you were shown Article 75 of that decree which stated that the funding would come from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then you were shown a second document which is just the next document in the binder, which was a similar decree but just dealing with primary education. Do you remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, then you were shown two documents emanating from Tuzla as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention just a practical thing. The reference to the first document, it was given by Mr. Kruger as 19, which is in fact 199. And then might I suggest it is helpful he refer to the next document. Not all of us have hard copy. I know what document he's talking about but I'm thinking about for the future when we're all looking at the transcripts months and months down the line to have the number of the exhibit on the transcript is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand fully. I take that on board. Thank you to my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, indeed, it is correct the document we were referring to first was 1D 00199. The document on primary education was 1D 00200. But then you were shown two documents emanating from Tuzla municipality, and these documents were shown to you on the basis that it shows that similar things were happening not only in Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna but also in other municipalities because it was alleged the central government in Sarajevo, the BiH government, Department of Education could not function outside its borders. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you to the first of the two documents that was then shown to you, 1D 00235. You have that document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is the decision of 19 October 1992: "Decision to take over the rights of founder with regard to the School of Commerce in Tuzla and transform it." Now, I'd like to refer you to Article 4 and there it says: "The School of Commerce shall obtain funds for its regular activities from the Republican Fund For Secondary Education in accordance with the criteria for distributing funds determined by the Fund's Managing Board ..." et cetera. During your evidence you referred to the Republican Fund. Is that the fund of the government of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For simple reasons I spoke only of the ministry; however, the distribution of funds went through the so-called SIZs. There was an -- they were funds. There was one such fund for schools which carried out financial transactions of this type. At the time we were referring to, the last salary paid from that fund was for April 1994 [as interpreted]. After that it did not pay a single salary for a long time. I don't know if it continued to exist so that in this case it could not pay the salaries for Tuzla. In these documents, this might have just been left there as these documents are usually copied from previous ones. But de facto there were no such payments. Perhaps whoever enacted this decision thought that the day would come when that fund would make the payments when it became possible. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to point out that on line 25 he said April 1994 and it should reflect 1992. And also my learned colleague, since he's trying to go about in this particular area regarding funding, in fairness to the witness he should point out to the witness Article 5, the first bulletin point. I think then the gentleman would be given a full opportunity to answer the question as opposed to cherry-picking one portion of the -- the decree that suits the Prosecutor's theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the bullet point that my learned colleague is referring to in Article 5, it says that: "The Tuzla Municipal Assembly shall provide in cooperation with the fund resources necessary ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour. It's working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, if I understand you correctly what you're saying is that you are of the opinion that this fund, the Republican Fund, the reference to it in this document is redundant?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to 1992, yes. At that point in time, it was redundant. I think it was redundant because to the best of my knowledge the last salaries were paid for April; and after that they ceased to arrive. April 1992 was the last month when salaries arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, from April onwards you weren't in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you didn't know or didn't have first-hand knowledge of what was going on in Sarajevo in the education department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion when I was in Zagreb I learned that Minister Hasic had managed to leave Sarajevo. His deputy, Professor Zukovic, had also left Sarajevo. The chief secretary had left Sarajevo. Half of the employees working in the ministry had left Sarajevo. I think almost all the employees who were Serbs had left the ministry, so at that time the ministry was unable to operate. Only a few people were left in it. In the course of the summer, later on, a new minister was appointed, Professor Kovac. But at that time the ministry did not really function and they told me the fund was not functioning either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But that's what you were told. You don't know about that from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from the head of the fund. I'm not sure that he was in Sarajevo. I know for a fact that at that time one could no longer leave Sarajevo and one could not operate in the manner required for work in the fund to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the documents that you were shown, that's P -- 1D, sorry, 00235 and 1D 00236, you needn't actually look at them, these are the two Tuzla documents, if I can refer to them like that. You weren't aware of the decision-making process or the processes involved in Tuzla municipality to bring these documents or to make -- which led to these decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So if you surmise that Article 4 is maybe just a cut-and-paste which was in error, you simply don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Article 4 in 1D 00235 or 236?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes -- I think the article is similar in both of the documents, but we were talking about the Article 4 in the first one earlier.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Monday we spoke about these two texts and compared them to texts of a similar provenance, that is, regulating education and schooling. We compared them on one level, which was that in cases such as these two cases the central government was quite simply isolated and unable to operate. In that case, someone else is taking over the rights of founder, someone who can function as such. That was what we discussed. The very fact that there was no communication with the central government had as its consequence that other entities took over the function of founder which was done in Tuzla, in Mostar, and later on in Jablanica in the documents that we used. This being the case, since there was a fund, the founder would not need to take over the responsibilities of founders in Tuzla and Mostar and other places, and the article that you are quoting, Article 4, this article follows from Article 1. In this case, it is contrary to Article 1. How can Tuzla be the founder if these things would be done by the central government which are typically done by the founder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I hear your argument but the question was still: You weren't in Tuzla and you don't know what the decision-making process was which led to this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. None of us was in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move on to another aspect, and for this if we can go to document P 00312. And I -- it's -- it was a Defence document but I've included it in the Prosecution binder. It's actually the first document in both binders if I'm not mistaken. Now, sir, you remember --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is the report of the 12 July 1992 meeting with President Tudjman, and you were present as well as various ministers from BiH and certain other people too. I'd like to refer you to page 7 of this document again, and specifically to where President Tudjman is talking about the H-O-S or the HOS. Do you have that portion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's not on page 7 in my version but I'll try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's directly after Mr. Z. Cosic has spoken and just before Mr. Manolic speaks.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you remember that -- sorry, just to refresh everybody's memory. This is where President Tudjman says: "We need Herceg-Bosna. We do not recognise HOS - they are the provocateurs of the former Independent State of Croatia and we do not accept this." Now, Judge Antonetti, the President, he asked you about this independent state of Croatia on Monday. Now, if we could perhaps clarify that a little bit further, is it correct that the independent state of Croatia was also known as the NDH?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge did not ask me about the NDH because I couldn't tell him much about that, but this is known what you ask me. Yes, this is the acronym for the independent state of Croatia, but I would like to say something before I start discussing this document, if I may. This document is a transcript, obviously, that is not an original. It can be seen in several elements. The language spoken by the participants seems as a language translated or maybe it was just a matter of poor transcription of what was spoken in a certain form. The forms of words, linguistics constructions are attributed to certain persons here who never in their statements or in their written works expressed themselves in that way. That's one thing. Another thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for purposes of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. We're going to come back to this document in a while. At this stage I just want to focus specifically on this portion and just clear up the independent state of Croatia first. Is it correct that this state existed from 1941 until 1945?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It was a puppet Nazi state which was established when the Nazis or the German army marched into Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I don't know the details when the German army entered. I did not deal with recent history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But it was established around about - would you agree? - 15 April 1941 by Slavko Kvaternik?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Ante Pavlovic then became the leader or the president of this state?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The NDH --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The NDH, it followed on after the existence of the Croatian Banovina which existed from 1939 to 1941; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly can't tell you about the dates in modern history. I did not deal with that period. If you state so, that's entirely possible. But I don't know those dates, they don't mean much to me, I did not deal with that period in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, just to continue with this, you wouldn't disagree that the Croatian Banovina was set up by the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement of 1939 which set it up as a Croatian province of the former Kingdom of Yugoslavia; correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- excuse me, excuse me, sir. If we could get sort of some relevance of this. What is the purpose of this cross-examination? Obviously, the gentleman is not a historian. He came here to discuss issues of education, language, et cetera, which he was involved in. Granted, he's being pointed out to a transcript dealing with HOS, but I fail to see the relevance between what was happening between 1941 to 1945 or before or thereafter, so perhaps if he could clarify that point I may not have to object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's wait and see. Let's wait for the other questions put by Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't dwell long upon this, but it is relevant, Your Honour, I submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you -- or do you know or have an idea of what territory the NDH comprised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe it comprised the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, most of the territory of the current Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I said, I did not deal with that. Maybe I supposed to know that, but I'm not certain of these things and allow me not to know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No, I'm not holding it against you, sir. So you said that Bosnia-Herzegovina, virtually the whole territory, was incorporated into this territory of the NDH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Meaning that Sarajevo was included in the territory, Banja Luka, for instance, Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to just show you a map and if you could perhaps just confirm that what you see is a map of the NDH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, this has not been given a Prosecution exhibit number, but if the witness confirms this we would propose that it be given an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, could you please tell us where this map comes from, which book?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Your Honour, this map was found on a web site and I unfortunately don't have the web address with me, but if I recall it's www.hercegbosna.com and the English part of that, but I will obtain it and provide it to my learned colleagues and to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful for that. May I also ask my learned friend to provide us with a legible copy. I can't make out the key at the bottom, and in fact that may be useful to the map, I don't know, at this stage. A clear, legible copy would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, the key -- we can't really see the key at the bottom, the colours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't mean to be obstructive here, but the gentleman indicated that he's not sufficiently knowledgeable about this area or this period or the details. Now he's being asked to confirm a map. Granted, we're dealing with professional Judges, but surely -- and this will be factored in, but how can the gentleman confirm something if a proper foundation hasn't been established? The gentleman has indicated he's insufficiently familiar with the period. Now he's being asked to validate the borders of a map. If this is a notorious fact, he can just put the question to him and then maybe establish this notorious fact later on through other evidence and through some other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, please put your question. There's a map coming from the internet. We don't really know where it comes from. On this map we see that Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sarajevo are included in the Independent State of Croatia, 1941-1945. That's what everyone can see on this map. So please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to recognise what this map depicts, despite not being a specialist in that period of the history?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read what is written, but I do not understand some things on this map. I don't know what blue denotes, the green colour, in the present territory of the Republic of Croatia, for instance, the area of the town of Split. I'm much more familiar with the medieval period. This was the centre of the medieval state of Croatia, and now it is outside the state of Croatia. Could you tell me what this denotes, how it is possible that the NDH did not comprise Split, Sibenik, the island of Korcula. This is unclear to me. This map doesn't make sense. I really cannot -- I'm confused. What I can tell you from general knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, this carte is not very clear for anyone, which is why I ask you to put your question that is going to support your case. Everyone sees that there are a lot of question marks, for example, on Split, it seems that Split is not included in the NDH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to obtain a better copy of the map or a better version of the map. Just to perhaps make a few things or clarify a few things which may assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct or did you know that parts of current-day Croatian territory were not included in the NDH? For instance, parts of Dalmatia and Istria, they were given to Italy, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Istria. It was occupied -- Italians occupied Istria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And we can actually see on this map in the top left-hand corner that there's the yellow part where the Istrian peninsula is and which is marked in yellow and not marked as part of the NDH.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, blue parts -- and we see in Slovenia there's a blue part. Is it correct that Germany occupied parts of Slovenia, do you know, during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they did, but I don't know about my own homeland, about my own country, so I'm not familiar with Slovenia. I generally heard about these things, but I never particularly dealt with recent history. If you ask -- wish to ask me questions relating to the Middle Ages, I would be in a much better position to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm still going to ask you two questions on this. The green areas are indicated on the key, if we look very hard, as Italian areas. Is it correct or did you hear, are you aware, that during the Second World War parts of this area were controlled by Italy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the key. Can you make it possible for me to see the key? Well, this is illegible, not useful at all. As a professor of literature, if I may say, there was this story which concerns the occupation of the island of Vis. So in any case, it is possible that the Italians occupied some parts, but I don't know which -- exactly which parts they did occupy - they did occupy some. I know about Zadar, they did occupy Zadar. They considered Zadar as part of Italy. I remember that, but as far as other areas occupied by them are concerned I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the whole purpose of this exercise of showing you the map was perhaps just to come to the point of: Is it correct that the HOS in 1992 had territorial aspirations to include the whole -- or which included the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. He needs to lay a foundation, and let me refer back to the way we began this cross-examination by referring to the documents in Tuzla. He was asking the gentleman whether, in fact, he was speculating as to the purposes for putting in Article 4. Now he's asking the gentleman without laying a foundation to speculate as to what HOS's intentions were. Unless he can establish some foundation that he was a member of HOS, participated with HOS, has knowledge of -- intimate knowledge of what HOS's policies and politics were, I don't believe he's capable of answering this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I put that question myself to the witness when we had the presidential transcript on the screen and where HOS was mentioned. The witness was at that meeting, so when Tudjman spoke about HOS if the witness had known nothing of HOS and HOS had not rung a bell, he could have -- he would have asked President Tudjman, Please give us some details, I don't understand what you're saying. But he didn't say so, so obviously he did have some notions about all this. Mr. Kruger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the question is: The HOS in 1992, were their territorial aspirations comparable to what we see in the NDH, including the -- in other words, including the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina up to the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say - and allow me to say what I know about that - people dressed in black uniforms with insignia HOS on their sleeves, with insignia which harked back to the NDH were worn by those soldiers. Nobody liked them. People -- I know none of them spoke with sympathies about the HOS. So when this was discussed at the meeting, the reaction there was normal when it came to the HOS. Apart from black uniforms, they would put pictures of figures who were compromised in the history on their vehicles. They would strut about trying to intimidate people, look frightening. I did not have any close contact with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there any talk at that stage about what these people were claiming territorially?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but, you know, if I may make this statement, you are evoking a very confusing time through your questions. My children, my family were most important. We were outside our homes. Thousands of others were also refugees, and at that time to think about what somebody else thought or to register such things of that type which when I hear them today do not make sense, they are illogical and even silly, stupid in a way, I simply did not register those at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before moving from this, final thing. President Tudjman says: "We need Herceg-Bosna." Do you know what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly because of the questions I suggested you may ask me, I think that the whole text should be read and those things which are omitted reflect more clearly the atmosphere in which this was discussed. What Tudjman is saying at that moment is the issue of collective subjectivity, and this is the issue which is known by those people who are sitting at the meeting. They are his party colleagues. He is saying that this should be done in the interests of the Croatian people which the Herceg-Bosna is supposed to protect. This was the only organization that at the time could protect the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is how everybody understood that and this is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to something else. Let's move back to Stolac in April 1992. Now, on Monday you testified - and this is a transcript reference in the provisional transcript page 17, lines 4 to 10 - you stated that the Croatian -- or the Crisis Staff agreed to evacuate the women, children, and elderly. And when they left, the HVO units who stayed, or the men who stayed in the positions, they melted from the field because the women, children, and elderly had gone. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, before exploring this I'd just like to clarify the concept of the Crisis Staff. You said - and this was at the transcript reference page 16 of the provisional transcript, pages [sic] 14 to 15 - you joined the Crisis Staff of the HVO. So this Crisis Staff, did it comprise only of HVO members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you a member or did you then become a member of the HVO by this action?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that point I was not member of the HVO. I must tell you, I don't know, I'm not certain, whether I did become a member from that point onwards. Maybe I did, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you testified that when the refugees returned there weren't many Muslims amongst them, and you said this morning as well that it was the Croats who returned. So my question to you is that when the Stolac Crisis Staff of the HVO took the decision to evacuate Stolac, there weren't any Muslims or SDA members --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- involved in that decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Muslims in making that decision, but at that meeting it was decided that the neighbouring Muslims should be advised of that decision. It was a rash decision, an urgent decision. At that time, as far as I can recall, the SDA had already started cooperating with the Serb side -- forces, they started making arrangements with the Serb forces at Berkovic, a northern part of the municipality settled by Serbs, and in Ljubinje which is a municipality some 30 kilometres away or less. Later on it was confirmed that they had done so. They had contacts -- had communicated with Serb army representatives, and they guaranteed the Serbian forces, Serbian army, free passage through Stolac. So at that moment, although earlier there had been attempts to make arrangements for common defence, that at that time this was -- could not be decided, as far as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, a number of witnesses have testified about this event in Stolac, and a number of witnesses have indeed said that their neighbours told them, We are leaving, come along. But a number of other people testified that they simply did not hear that there was a decision to evacuate. And when they opened their eyes, their Croat neighbours had all left. Is it possible that this decision to invite the Muslims to also evacuate along with the Croats was not communicated properly or efficiently?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was I who proposed at that meeting that this be done. I personally, where my parents were living, I personally warned the Muslims in the neighbourhood. I know some other people did that at other places. I know also that a substantial number of neighbours did depart, some did not. They reached Pocitelj together with Croats, and at Pocitelj some people - I wasn't there, I was told about that - their compatriot, fellow countrymen, simply told them not to go further; and in most cases those people returned. Of course I say this with some reservations because later I heard and met some people in the place where my parents lived. I met some Muslims. So I allow for this possibility for them to have passed through there despite the suggestions to the contrary. The Muslims left Stolac at the moment when it was a liberated because there were -- there was combat and even before this Stolac was liberated. I personally met a large number of Muslim refugees at Metkovic, and that was a couple of days prior to Stolac's liberation. And at that time during combat operations some people fled to Pocitelj, Capljina, most of the people, women, children, the elderly fled there. I met some of them at Visici, at Pocitelj, it was then, sometime in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm -- I need to just ask you a few questions about this. I don't understand and I haven't heard before that Muslims left or a large number of Muslims left Stolac at the time of its liberation in June 1992. Can you give the Court an idea of the magnitude of this departure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain precisely how many people were involved, but at any rate - and I think I've already said that - Stolac and Mostar and the towns in Herzegovina are mostly situated in valleys, in the canyons of rivers. Stolac is all built in a valley. Overlooking Stolac there are hills on which there were artillery positions and mortar positions of the Serbian army. One morning when I was on my way to Stolac, I went to a village called Osanici overlooking Stolac which was also liberated, and Stolac was full of red mushrooms because there was mortar fire going on. The roofs were all of red tiles and the roofs being blown up looked like red mushrooms. It was a horrifying picture. One could not continue living there at the time, so people left. Before the attack I mentioned that some Muslims had got to Metkovic and been accommodated in the secondary school there, in the gym, and that food and beverages were distributed to them. I don't know for how long they stayed there, but they left before the liberation of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that they returned afterwards, after the liberation, most of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was possible; I can't tell you the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before stepping off this aspect, to the extent -- well, you were asked or you touched upon whether there was a defence or a mutual defence agreement, to paraphrase it perhaps, between the Muslims and the Croats prior to the entry of the Serbs or the take-over of the Serbs. And you said -- I don't have your exact words here, but you said there wasn't really a formal agreement such as that that you know of. Is that correct or am I characterizing it correctly, what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to agreements between the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake. The Muslims and the Croats prior to the Serb take-over in April 1992 of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo and I arrived only a short time before all this. I heard a lot of things from the people who had been there before. I knew a lot of people there as my fellow citizens. It was a small town, and all those representatives of the Croats were mostly organized in the HDZ party which had won the elections. All the representatives of the Muslims who were relevant at the time, those who were active in politics and who held positions in the authorities, they were in the SDA party. So at the time it was mostly these two parties that discussed agreements, but these agreements were of an informal nature. They discussed these things at the meetings of their leaderships. I doubt that they even had minutes, and I concluded all this on the basis of statements I heard later on and based on events which happened later on. But I was not present at those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From what you could gather in this way or what you saw, would it be fair to say that there was at least some informal understanding that a mutual defence would be mounted against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think there was that understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, when a few days after the women, children, and elderly, Croatian women, children, and elderly had left, when the Croatian men who were in the HVO melted away from their positions, that would actually be leaving the Muslim defenders in the lurch, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite the contrary. I can give you an example, something that sprang to my mind in the meantime, although maybe it's not something popular in courts. When my parents and those other people had to leave the area, when they came to the river Neretva because they couldn't cross the bridge, as the bridge had been blocked by the Serbian forces, we were very worried. In Pocitelj they had to cross the river Neretva using various makeshift devices. At one point we were in the MUP, which was actually the police station, and there were representatives of both Croats and Muslims there. At that point a young man arrived, his name was Skrba, and he was a guard in the VP Dom. He arrived from the area controlled by the Serbs and he was looking for the local chief of the SDA Alija Rizvanbegovic, the president of the party in that area, to tell him that they were waiting for him overlooking -- at a place overlooking Stolac, that the president of the SDS party, the Serb party, and some other people were waiting for him there. I asked him, Who else is there? And they said Milan Mihic. He was a doctor. I knew those people. We had been schoolmates before. I asked, Can I go when Alija goes? And he said, Well, there's no reason for you not to go. And then the president of the municipality who was the mayor, Raguz, also went. The two of us went with this young man, as did Alija Rizvanbegovic, and we arrived at a certain location. Alija Rizvanbegovic, the chief of the SDA, did not join in our conversation while we were there, but he stayed behind after we had left. I asked my colleague, Milan Mihic, to call his colleagues from the SDS, from the Capljina area and ask them to let those people cross the Neretva. And Milan Mihic accompanied me to the MUP, to the police station, and the telephones were still operating at the time. He made a phone call. I listened to the conversation, and the man said he would do it. Then the president of the SDA remained talking to the representatives of the Serb authorities, and I don't know what they discussed. But in any case, this led me to believe the rumours I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But, sir, if I can return just briefly to the original question. Your choice of words was interesting. "The HVO melted away from their positions ..." Is it correct that when they melted away they left their positions undefended, unoccupied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to object to these questions by my learned friend for the following reasons. The questions refer to early April 1992, which is the period before the Serb occupation, and they presume that there were HVO units holding positions and also that there were military units of some Muslim army. So the issue would be that HVO units retreated before the Serb aggression without putting up any resistance. This, however, is not supported by a single shred of evidence in this case, nor did the witness ever say that there was an organized HVO army in March and early April 1992. I think it's very important to clarify this point because this sequence of questions might mislead us to believe that organized HVO units fled before the JNA and the Serbs assaulting Stolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, I confess that I did not quite see what you were aiming at, but you're doing your cross-examination so I'll leave you to answer -- to ask questions. Regarding Ms. Alaburic's remark, the two possibilities, either there are HVO units and Muslim units prior to April 1992; you then should ask the witness who knows Stolac and the wider area whether he was aware of the units. He will say yes or no, and depending on his answer you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was asking the question based on the testimony of the witness, and if I can refer to the transcript of Monday, the provisional numbering is page 17 and it's at line 10, 9 to 10 -- line 10. "The HVO units simply melted from the field ..." Those were the words of the witness, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, I have actually finished with this point so I'll move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's go back to the infamous document that you've had a look at previously, P 00312, the report of 12 July 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the word "infamous." Why is it so infamous? I mean -- a notorious context to it. There's nothing nefarious about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I withdraw that. It's a bad choice of words, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It was referring to -- it comes up a lot in these proceedings today and Monday. Sir, if you look it should be the first document in the Defence binder but it's also the first document in the Prosecution binder, P 00312. You have it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, my first question is that if we look at who's attending this meeting from the BiH side there are ministers, ministers of the BiH, and then you were there, a deputy minister. So this was an official BiH delegation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, that's certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Why do you say "in part"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, the people in this delegation were also members of the Presidency and the party of the HDZ, or rather, the HDZ party Presidency, apart from me -- except for me, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you, who did you represent at that meeting then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was part of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while the others were both that and members of the Presidency of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Professor Brkic at the time was the president of the HDZ. Mate Boban was a member of the Presidency. Iko Stanic was a member of the Presidency. I don't know whether there were any other members of the Presidency there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look on the first page it says - and this is in the -- it says: "From the official trip to Zagreb ..." et cetera? And then the next paragraph: "Together with Mr. Brkic, Krsticevic ..." et cetera. And then it says: "... upon the instruction of the BH prime minister ..." Who was that, was that Mr. Izetbegovic? Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's on the very first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for my learned friend's edification, Mr. Izetbegovic was never the prime minister as far as I understand. Mr. Jure Pelivan was the prime minister at the time. Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency. There is a big distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have that, sir? It's on the first page, and I think it's the second paragraph which starts with: "Skupa sa gosp. Brkic ..." "Together with Mr. Brkic ..."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it now, that's the second paragraph in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the BH minister, is that then -- or prime minister, is that then Mr. Jure Pelivan at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Jure Pelivan was the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was your mandate? What -- did you receive a mandate from him for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was given a mandate. It was just a discussion, it was just talks, exchanging information, providing information about what was happening on the ground. If you look at the rest of the transcript you'll see that it's quite clear. Whoever transcribed this left out some things which they considered unimportant, but without those parts you can misunderstand the text and misinterpret it. In order to interpret it correctly, you really need to have the whole because sometimes replies put forward by certain participants refer to those missing parts of the text and they reveal the emotional background, the real reasons why some people did not agree to something. Very often these are very personal things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt again. I'm told that there was a mistranslation. The question was rightly put whether -- as I understood it, whether the gentleman received a mandate from Jure Pelivan, that was I believe the intention of my learned friend. It was translated whether he received a mandate, that is, at the meeting, hence the answer, which may give the appearance that he's being less than truthful or evasive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, let us avoid wasting time and let us avoid objections. It looks as though the answer you were seeking was given by Mr. Brkic on page 2 in the English version. He thanked Mr. Tudjman for making the meeting possible and for inviting them, so apparently he was invited or they were invited by Mr. Tudjman. That's what Mr. Brkic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's indeed in the text. Is it correct that your delegation was invited by President Tudjman to this meeting? And it would be the first place where Mr. Brkic speaks in your text, first line.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the text, but I'm not sure who organized the meeting. In any case, a sentence like this is a significant piece of protocol. It shows respect for your guests. If you have been invited, then you are of great consequence; if you are the one who asked to be received, it's different. So this has to do with diplomatic relations, with protocol, and I think there's this semantic segment in the sentence -- but actually, I don't know, I'm not aware. It would be Milenko Brkic and Jure Pelivan who could answer your question precisely. I was just there and everyone had been given this document except me, as you can see, because I was not a party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, let's explore whether this was only an exchange indeed of information. Mr. Brkic - and this is still on page 2 where he speaks - do you recall that he asked President Tudjman about what is the -- what is Herceg-Bosna, what is the HVO, what is the scope of the authority of the HVO? Can you recall that he asked such questions there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recall all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, why would he be asking these questions of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although Greek Heraclitus said that -- anyway, I have to guess here, I have to speculate. The main dialogue was not conducted with Tudjman. The main dialogue was between Brkic and Boban. Brkic spoke first because he was the party chief. Boban was the HVO president. So there was certain relations and certain disagreement among the two of them. Mr. Brkic's questions were rhetorical. He was setting forth his position at that point, trying to say something about his position as the top man who was perhaps not at that point feeling that he was the top man because of certain objections which can be gleaned from the text and from the discourse of Boban who begins in anger saying: "If I had known such things would be said, I wouldn't have come ..." So you can see that this is, in fact, a dialogue between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So do you think that Mr. Brkic was therefore expecting answers to these questions to come from this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It calls for speculation, Your Honour. Surely -- I mean how is he to divine what the gentleman wanted? Surely if I was posing the question, I would be getting objections left and right and perhaps from the Bench as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, the witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, do stick to facts, to certainties. If you ask him to interpret Mr. Brkic's position, he did say that between Brkic and Boban there was no total agreement, they did not see eye to eye. So it seems that he therefore knows Mr. Brkic and knows Mr. Boban very well too, I don't know. But try to move on solid ground; otherwise, you're going to have objections from Mr. Karnavas, it's going to be time wasted. Go straight -- cut to the quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, let's cut to the quick then and turn to page 8, and it's page 8 in both the English and the B/C/S version, so your version is also page 8. Do you have page 8?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who is speaking? I do have page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if you can look at where Mr. T. Krsticevic speaks and he says: "I would like to know whether BH has been order - the dinar as the official BH currency - and what our attitude should be. I'd like an answer on that." Here we have a concrete demand for an answer. Isn't it so, sir, that this meeting was actually there to provide answers for various questions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, as you can see, Mr. Krsticevic, who was the minister of communications and transport in the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was tasked by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do certain things by Mr. Jure Pelivan who was the prime minister. One of those tasks was to print money to be the legal tender in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Sarajevo. That money was printed and later transported and brought there, but as Mr. Krsticevic as an expert in monetary matters and cognizant of the situation at the time because at the time the Yugoslav dinar was still in circulation there were still huge losses created then with Yugoslav dinar, I don't know much about that. But I know what my father lost then in banks -- banks went down, everything went down. It's far away from the situation in Wall Street today. It was a complete collapse. And at the time when money is not worth anything, where there is no backing for the money, then it is only logical that a person like Krsticevic would ask the question, What should we do? He most probably asked that of other colleagues with whom he had occasion to discuss. He sought every opportunity to hear relevant people telling me and discussing these matters and I'm sure he related that to Mr. Jure Pelivan and the others he met subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll adjourn now and have a break. So far you've used an hour and a 25 minutes more or less. So we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court's back in session. I believe Mr. Scott would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning to you, Mr. President, to all of the Judges, good morning. Sorry to be behind the pole. My apologies to, in particular Judge Prandler. Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting the flow of the witness. I know we have a witness on the stand, but I think it's absolutely essential that I raise something procedural so that we can hopefully schedule it and allow time to resolve it or to address it at the -- before the end of today's session because I know the Chamber said we would end at 1.20 today, if I'm not mistaken, instead of 1.45. Your Honour, I'm going to say the next couple of things generically. I'm not going to mention the witness's name because we're in public session. I don't think that's an issue at this moment, but the Prosecution has filed this morning a motion concerning next week's witness. Again, I will not mention the witness by name. That will be distributed by -- that's been filed as a courtesy to the Judges, to you and to the courtroom and to counsel, that will be distributed so that we can take it up, hopefully, later today. The nature of the motion and the relief requested by the Prosecution, Your Honour, concerning next week's witness is that once again the Prosecution finds it has been provided an inadequate summary, inadequate information concerning the witness. This has been a continuing problem. The Prosecution seeks to have the witness stricken, to strike the witness from the witness list, to preclude the witness from testifying, or in the alternative, the Prosecution finally receive a meaningful summary of what this witness's actual evidence will be. Now, I raise it today because presumably depending on the Chamber's ruling we can hopefully or possibly, let me say possibly, prevent the witness from travelling unnecessarily if the Chamber rules today, so he doesn't have to get on a plane and come from Bosnia until this matter can be resolved. I would like to reserve enough time toward the end of the day prior to 1.20 so this can be addressed on its merits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President, just so that we're clear. I received a letter from the Prosecution, I responded, I indicated to them also that I would -- they wanted some specific information. I indicated that I would get back to them. I contacted the witness and got some additional information and provided that information to the Prosecution. So this is the first I hear subsequent to that that they wanted additional information. But again, once I got their request at the first available moment I responded. I then made contact with the witness through our investigator to get more specific information and provided that to the Prosecution based on the questions that they were raising. So we did act in good faith. Now, if they wanted some additional information, I don't know what it is, I'm sure I'll find out in reading their pleading, but in any event we did try to act accordingly and based on what was being requested of us. If it was insufficient, then we'll -- I guess we'll have to argue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. All that's addressed in the motion. My understanding was we would not address the merits at this time to argue our cases. To respond ever so briefly to Mr. Karnavas since he has jumped ahead to the merits, Your Honour, the Prosecution has repeatedly -- this has been a recurring problem. This is not new to Mr. Karnavas or anyone in the courtroom. This has been a recurring problem with the witnesses that have been presented. We've asked repeatedly. We did indeed send a letter. We made a number of inquiries. You know, you can only ask so many times. We get to the time now that it's only a few days before the witness is scheduled to appear and we have still not received the information required by the Rules and I do ask the Chamber to allow time for us to address this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have your memo here sent on September 19, 2008, to Prosecution, and in this memo you give additional information but that's quite -- there's not much. You are reminding things that you already said in the summary, there's not much new and additional information which is why we have this request. Could you do something by the end of the week? Could you provide the Prosecution by the end of the week with a better resume, a longer resume, a longer summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you look at the letter dated September 9, they pose three or -- three particular questions. I had been approached by Mr. Stringer a couple of times and I had told him a couple of times that the gentleman -- because they wanted to know what his status was in the HVO, we told them that he was a simple soldier, did not hold a particular position once he joined the HVO. So you will see on 18 September 2008 I sent a brief note because they wanted verification. I also informed them at that time that I would make contact with the witness in order to get more specific information based on the three questions that they asked. Based on the questions asked, we received additional information to which then I forwarded almost the next day, 19 September, where I provided the detailed information. I don't -- I seriously do not know what it is that the Prosecution wants, and I frankly find it really troublesome that we have high-paying [sic] prosecutors, highly experienced, that are claiming that they are incapable of knowing how to cross-examine a simple witness such as this one based on the information and keeping in mind that they've had ten years to investigate this case. I really have a hard time understanding that. They prosecuted this entire case in that region, they would have known of this individual, they could have done their background information. They want me to do their work. I'm sorry; I will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, let's not waste any time. The important thing is the witness we have at the moment. I see that you have asked four hours for this witness. I believe that in that four -- in those four hours you will present them a lot of documents. You probably have a work-plan, you know, as you usually have and this is what the Prosecutor would like to have, would like to know what points you're going to address with this witness. Of course I understand that you're quite reluctant to provide this information but it would be simpler. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't want to truncate my arguments to the Prosecution's prejudice. What I've asked several times is, with great respect to the Chamber and to the witness, that we set this over until the end of today's session, allow enough time; but every time Mr. Karnavas gets on his feet, he argues his case. Now, as Judge Trechsel observed several weeks ago, we've seen again this morning what Mr. Karnavas so often does. When question arises or something comes up, he immediately attacks and criticizes the other side. This issue has nothing, has nothing to do with the experience of Prosecution counsel or our ability or what we do, our ability to do our jobs. The Rules require the Defence to provide this information, not for the Prosecution or the Chamber to guess as to what the witness's testimony might be. So I don't -- I'm tired of these attacks. I'm tired of all these attacks. When it's Mr. Karnavas, with great respect, that does not fulfill his obligations under the law. It has nothing to do with Prosecution counsel. Again, Your Honour -- I see another counsel on their feet. Can we set this off until some time, approximately 1.00, so we can address it at the end of the day and not keep the witness out of the courtroom any longer or are we going to argue it now? I'm happy to argue it now, but let's do it one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I am counsel with the same rights of audience as my learned friend Mr. Scott. The only reason I was rising to my feet was to state that there's no need, I think, for temperature to rise in this courtroom. There is a written motion that's before you and I certainly would support my learned friend Mr. Scott that perhaps this matter can be put back and it can be argued at the end of the day. I rose in a spirit of cooperation. It wasn't a matter that should have got beneath the skin of my learned friend, and I'm sorry if it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is what we'll do. We will finish this cross-examination. I believe we only have about an hour left or so, Mr. Kruger has about an hour left, not more. And then we'll deal with this problem at the end of the session. Mr. Stewart, you will have the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wanted to say that by supporting what Mr. Khan's just said, we all have at least the right to intervene on any of these matters and to know what's going on. So any relevant material for this particular discussion which is going to take place must be made available to all concerned in at least enough time for us to be able to look at it. So it may be that it's all going around right now, but as a matter of principle that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, and we will deal with the matter later on after we are finished with this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there should have been a copy provided to each of the Judges and also to counsel. If it hasn't been distributed yet, my apologies. My instructions -- my request had been -- and I realise everyone's busy --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it has, as it happens, so I think we're all on the same hymn sheet on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Khan. Witness, the cross-examination will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, just to briefly return to the map that was previously shown, I have just ascertained that it is already in evidence as P 09536 and it's page 62 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break we were looking at what Mr. Krsticevic had said. He asked about -- what about the currency, the BH money. I'd like an answer to that. But it's correct, isn't it, that at that very meeting President Tudjman actually expressed his opinion on that money, and I refer you to page 6 of the transcript. President Tudjman says on page 6 and I'll just read it to you: "As far as money is concerned in BH as long as the dinar is not accepted in the entire region you too should not accept it and I have personal and historical experience in this regard." So President Tudjman, he expressed his view, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find that passage. You claim that it was on a preceding page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On page 6 and it's about a third from the top. It starts with [B/C/S spoken], sorry for my pronunciation. Sir, the page numbering is in the middle below the text and there should be a number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I could request the usher to perhaps assist the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So it's correct that President Tudjman did give his opinion and view that the BH dinar should not be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As for the currency in BH, until dinar is not widely accepted in the whole territory you do not have to accept it either and I do have personal historical experience of that." Well, I can see that this is written here. I cannot recall every statement made there. Yes, what was your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So President Tudjman did express his view on it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he did not say, Do not accept the money. Because in your first question you said that he advised that the currency should not be accepted, but this sentence reads: "Until all the others in Bosnia-Herzegovina accept, you should not ..." At that time it was -- it shouldn't -- this money should not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, he's telling this to the ministers of another state whose currency that is; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a currency, as far as I knew, was a replacement for dinar. It was a currency of sorts --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, if I can interrupt you. The people at that meeting included ministers of another state, not the Republic of Croatia; and he's telling those ministers of BiH to not accept the currency of BiH provisionally until the certain things occur. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He expresses his opinion that this currency should not be accepted under those circumstances because he has some historical experience that it wouldn't be advisable to accept it under such circumstances. He expresses and relates his experience. He's not ordering anybody. He's expressing his opinion. He's not saying you shouldn't or you mustn't. He's saying, There's no need for you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just above that piece he also says: "The system of authority being created by Kljuic and Doko is not for us. For us, the core of authority must lie in the HDZ." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he's saying this to a meeting of largely HDZ members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now let's turn to page -- let me just find this. This page does not have a number, but if you look in the top right-hand corner of the documents you will see a number 0420 and then 1248. So look in the top right-hand corner for page 1248, and that's the page where the conclusions start or are contained. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph above the conclusions, Mr. Manolic speaks. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. And then Mr. Manolic expresses the following and he says -- and that's about the second sentence in: "The party of HDZ is above HVO and civilian administration. Whenever the government has been ruined temporarily, bodies can be established, legally elected authorities must not be touched." Now, he says the party of HDZ is above the HVO. So that's in actual fact how he put it, the HDZ set the policy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object or I'm going to ask for clarification. Is he asking to validate what Manolic is saying or is he asking what he actually knows? There is a distinction. We can all read the transcript. So which is -- which of it is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what were you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can move on it will become clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I don't want to move on. I raised an objection. I won, now let's go back to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, are you asking for the witness to validate what Mr. Manolic said or are you asking him what he infers from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you were at this meeting. Was that your understanding, that this is actually what the situation was, the HDZ sets policy and the HVO follows?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to say something else before I specifically answer your question. I really thought that you asked me whether it is true that Manolic said that. I don't know and can't recall what he said, but it's written here. You also said a minute ago that this went for representatives of another country. It is true, but it's also true that they are members of the HDZ. I had an opportunity to start discussing this way of expressing - when we say "we," it means an expression, opinion, within the political party, the HDZ - and the question that you asked about money that should not be accepted, that was a suggestion to fellow party members. Two levels are being mixed here. I, as a witness, and probably other witnesses as well, have problems with the statements because we're not used to legal codifications where there are no rhetorical figures, no metaphors. Things are transformed into terms, expressions, and these are traps for witnesses, pitfalls for them. So please do not force me into a pitfall. This is not a usual situation for me. I'm really trying to answer all your questions with full sincerity and to the best of my knowledge. In this case I do not know what Mr. Manolic thought. I wasn't a party member so that I could learn that. He did say that on that occasion. It seems to me that discussions were held at the level of the political party first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if -- let's look at the conclusions which will perhaps make this even clearer. The conclusions, 1, do you have point 1? "Role of HDZ in newly emerged circumstances." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the third bullet point says: "In the newly emerged circumstances decisions of the party Presidency also have the value of decisions of Assembly and are binding for all party organs, party representatives in all governing bodies and all members." So --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- does this -- is it true that what is being said here is that the HDZ leadership, which is with President Tudjman at the top, they set the policy for everything which falls under this party of HDZ?
